title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 20
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

parts.title: Problem Solving
parts.description: A conversation in which one person has a problem and seeks help from another.

parts.title: Daily Life Conversation
parts.description: An everyday conversation between two people.

parts.title: Listening for Information
parts.description: An informational talk; listen for specific details.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.description: A discussion among people with different viewpoints.

parts.title: Viewpoints
parts.description: A longer talk presenting one speaker's opinion and reasons.

listeningScripts.title: A Dental Bill After a Coverage Change
listeningScripts.text: Caller: I've had a bill for four hundred and sixty dollars for a crown. I thought my plan covered it. Clinic: Let me look. The treatment date was the second of October? Caller: That's right. Clinic: And your employer's plan changed on the first of October. Your old plan covered crowns at eighty per cent. The new one covers them at fifty, with a twelve-month waiting period for major work. Caller: Nobody told me about a waiting period. Clinic: That would have come from your employer or from the insurer rather than from us. But here is the part that matters. The waiting period applies to new members. If you were continuously covered under the old plan with no gap, most insurers will waive it. It's called a transfer credit, and it is not automatic. Somebody has to ask for it. Caller: How do I ask? Clinic: Through your HR department, not the insurer directly. They confirm the continuous coverage and the insurer applies the credit. It usually takes about three weeks. Caller: And if they apply it? Clinic: Then the crown is covered at fifty per cent rather than nothing, so the bill drops from four hundred and sixty to two hundred and thirty. It does not go back to eighty. The new plan's percentage is the new plan's percentage. Caller: Do I pay in the meantime? Clinic: I would ask us to hold the account for six weeks, which we will do on request. Don't simply not pay it. After sixty days it goes to a collections file automatically, and pulling it back out of there is much harder than never sending it. Caller: Can you make the note now? Clinic: Doing it as we speak. Six weeks from today, and if you tell us HR is still working on it, I can extend it once.

listeningScripts.title: Sharing a Skip
listeningScripts.text: A: I'm getting a skip for the garage clear-out. Do you want half of it? B: How much is a skip? A: Three hundred and ten for a six-yard, delivered Friday, collected Monday. B: So a hundred and fifty-five each. That's less than two trips to the tip in petrol and a Saturday. A: That's the idea. It goes on my drive, so you would be carrying across. B: That's fine, it's twenty metres. What can't go in it? A: No paint, no tyres, no electricals, no mattresses. The mattress is the one that catches people. They charge forty on top if there's one in there. B: I have a mattress. A: Then that's a separate trip, and it's genuinely worth doing separately, because the tip takes mattresses free. B: Right. What about the fridge in my shed? A: Electrical. Same answer. B: This skip is starting to feel less useful. A: It's useful for the eight cubic metres of nothing-in-particular that neither of us can face sorting. That is what it is for. B: Fair enough. Load it Saturday morning? A: Saturday morning. And we fill it level, not heaped, or they refuse to take it away.

listeningScripts.title: Neighbourhood Emergency Preparedness
listeningScripts.text: Thanks for coming out on a wet evening. I have twenty minutes and I want to spend it on the things that are actually different from what you would guess. First, the seventy-two hours. You have all heard the figure. What people picture is food, and food is the easy part — most households have three days of food without trying. Water is where households fail. Four litres per person per day, and that is drinking and washing together, so for a family of four across three days it is forty-eight litres. That is a great many bottles, and it is why we suggest containers rather than bottles. Second, your gas shut-off. If you don't know where it is, that is tonight's job. And do not turn it off as a precaution. Turn it off only if you smell gas or the building has moved, because once it is off it has to be turned back on by the utility, and after a large event that has taken people two weeks. Third, the meeting point. Every household should have two: one outside the house, and one outside the neighbourhood. The second matters more, because the failure case is not a house fire. It is not being able to get back into the area at all. Fourth, text rather than call. Calls fail when the network is loaded. Texts queue and go through. Same network, different behaviour. Fifth, the block list. There are twenty-one households on this street and we know eleven of them by name. Nobody is asking you to become friends. We are asking you to write down who might need help getting down stairs. And finally, whatever you buy tonight, put a date in your phone a year from now to check it. Batteries and water both go off, and an emergency kit that nobody has opened since twenty-nineteen is a box of disappointments.

listeningScripts.title: Alberta Caps Early-Grade Class Sizes
listeningScripts.text: Alberta will cap class sizes at twenty-two students from kindergarten through grade three, beginning next September, with funding for about nine hundred additional teachers. The cap does not apply above grade three, which the province says reflects the evidence: the effect of smaller classes is largest in the earliest grades and fades as students get older. School boards welcomed the funding but raised two practical problems. The first is space. A smaller class needs a room, and boards in the fastest-growing suburbs have no rooms left, which means portables and a capital cost the announcement does not cover. The second is recruitment: nine hundred teachers is more than the province's faculties graduate in a year. The teachers' association said the cap should have applied to grade four and above as well, but described it as a genuine improvement rather than a token one. Compliance will be measured on the thirtieth of September each year, a date some boards say invites a class to be balanced for one day and then left alone. The province said it will also sample twice during the year without notice.

listeningScripts.title: A Crossing or a Speed Table
listeningScripts.text: Sindhu: Two options outside the school, and we can afford one. A signalled crossing at thirty-eight thousand, or a raised speed table at nine. Oduya: They do different things. The crossing gives children a protected place to cross. The table slows everybody, everywhere along that stretch, including the drivers who never stop at a crossing anyway. Ntuli: My children don't cross there. They cross forty metres up, at the corner, because that is where the path comes out. If you put the crossing where the plan shows it, they will still cross at the corner, and they will be crossing next to a crossing that isn't there. Sindhu: Can we move the crossing to the corner? Oduya: Not to the corner itself — sight lines. Ten metres back from it, yes, and that is a better location than the one on the plan. Ntuli: Then that is a real question. Ten metres back is still not where the path comes out. Oduya: No. And here is the honest answer. A crossing works when people use it, and people use it when it is on their line. Move a crossing twenty metres off somebody's line and a third of them will not walk to it. Sindhu: Whereas the table works whether anybody cooperates or not. Oduya: That is the argument for it. It is also the argument against thinking it is enough on its own. Ntuli: I would take the table, and the twenty-nine thousand we haven't spent, and I would ask what a footpath from the corner to the crossing point costs. Oduya: Under ten thousand. That I could get done in the same season. Sindhu: Then the table plus the path, and the crossing goes on next year's list with the path already built.

listeningScripts.title: Calorie Counts on Menus
listeningScripts.text: Several countries now require calorie counts on menus in the larger chains, and the policy has been running long enough that we can stop arguing about what might happen and look at what did. What happened is small. The best studies — the ones comparing chains that were covered against chains that were not — find a reduction of somewhere between twenty and eighty calories per meal. That is real, it is measurable, and it is roughly one bite of a burger. Set against the scale of the problem it is close to nothing, and anybody who told you this policy would move the needle was overselling it. But here is the part that changed my view. The measurable effect on customers is small. The effect on the menus themselves is not. Chains that came under the rules reformulated. They cut portion sizes, they changed recipes, and several of them quietly withdrew their highest-calorie items rather than print the number beside them. One study found that the average calorie count of newly introduced items fell by about a quarter after the rules came in. The customers barely changed what they ordered. The restaurants changed what there was to order. That is a genuinely different mechanism from the one the policy was sold on, and it is the more durable of the two, because it does not depend on anybody reading anything. The cost worth naming is the one that falls on people with eating disorders, for whom an unavoidable number attached to every item is a documented harm. That is not a reason to abandon the policy, but it is a reason to stop pretending the policy is free. So: keep it, defend it on the supply side rather than the demand side, and stop citing the calories-per-meal figure as though it were the point.

questions.prompt: Why is the caller telephoning?
options: Her treatment was carried out on the wrong date
She has been charged twice for the same crown
Her dental plan has been cancelled without notice
She has been billed for a crown she expected to be covered
questions.correctAnswer: She has been billed for a crown she expected to be covered
questions.explanation: The caller has a four hundred and sixty dollar bill for a crown she believed her plan covered.

questions.prompt: What changed on the first of October?
options: The clinic's fees
Her employer's plan
The date of her treatment
The insurer's assessment of the crown
questions.correctAnswer: Her employer's plan
questions.explanation: The employer's plan changed on the first of October, the day before the treatment, taking crown coverage from eighty per cent to fifty.

questions.prompt: What does the new plan add?
options: A twelve-month wait before major work is covered
A limit on the number of crowns
A requirement to use an approved clinic
A higher annual premium
questions.correctAnswer: A twelve-month wait before major work is covered
questions.explanation: The new plan covers crowns at fifty per cent and imposes a twelve-month waiting period for major work.

questions.prompt: Who does the clinic say should have told her about the waiting period?
options: The clinic, before the treatment
The dentist who fitted the crown
Her employer or the insurer
Nobody, because it applies automatically
questions.correctAnswer: Her employer or the insurer
questions.explanation: The clinic says notice of the waiting period would have come from the employer or the insurer rather than from the practice.

questions.prompt: What is a transfer credit?
options: A discount for paying the bill in full
A payment from the old insurer to the new one
A credit towards next year's treatment
A waiver of the waiting period for somebody continuously covered
questions.correctAnswer: A waiver of the waiting period for somebody continuously covered
questions.explanation: Most insurers waive the waiting period where cover has been continuous with no gap — a transfer credit, which is not automatic and has to be asked for.

questions.prompt: Who should the caller approach?
options: Her HR department
The insurer's claims line
The clinic's billing office
Her previous insurer
questions.correctAnswer: Her HR department
questions.explanation: The request goes through HR rather than to the insurer directly: HR confirms the continuous coverage and the insurer then applies the credit, in about three weeks.

questions.prompt: What will the bill become if the credit is applied?
options: Nothing at all
Ninety-two dollars
Two hundred and thirty dollars
Four hundred and sixty dollars
questions.correctAnswer: Two hundred and thirty dollars
questions.explanation: The credit removes the waiting period but not the new percentage, so the crown is covered at fifty per cent and the bill halves to two hundred and thirty.

questions.prompt: Why should she not simply leave the bill unpaid?
options: Interest is added from the first month
After sixty days it goes automatically to collections
The clinic would refuse further treatment
The insurer would reject the claim
questions.correctAnswer: After sixty days it goes automatically to collections
questions.explanation: The clinic will hold the account for six weeks on request, but an unpaid bill goes automatically to a collections file after sixty days, and retrieving it from there is much harder.

questions.prompt: What does A suggest?
options: Borrowing B's car for a trip to the tip
Clearing the garage together on Saturday
Splitting the cost of a skip
Hiring a van between them
questions.correctAnswer: Splitting the cost of a skip
questions.explanation: A is hiring a six-yard skip for three hundred and ten dollars and offers B half of it.

questions.prompt: What does B compare the cost to?
options: Two trips to the tip and a lost Saturday
The cost of hiring a van
What a skip cost last year
The council's collection charge
questions.correctAnswer: Two trips to the tip and a lost Saturday
questions.explanation: At a hundred and fifty-five each, B reckons it comes to less than two trips to the tip in petrol plus a Saturday.

questions.prompt: Which item does A say catches people out?
options: Paint, which is refused at the gate
Tyres, which are charged by weight
Anything electrical, which is fined
A mattress, which adds a charge of forty dollars
questions.correctAnswer: A mattress, which adds a charge of forty dollars
questions.explanation: Paint, tyres, electricals and mattresses are all excluded, but the mattress is the one that catches people, because it adds forty dollars if it is found in the skip.

questions.prompt: What does A suggest doing with B's mattress?
options: Leaving it beside the skip for collection
Taking it to the tip, which accepts mattresses free
Splitting the forty-dollar charge
Putting it in underneath the other waste
questions.correctAnswer: Taking it to the tip, which accepts mattresses free
questions.explanation: A separate trip is worth making because the tip takes mattresses at no charge, unlike the skip.

questions.prompt: Why must the skip be filled level?
options: It will not be collected otherwise
The weight limit is calculated by height
The neighbours have complained before
A heaped skip costs more to empty
questions.correctAnswer: It will not be collected otherwise
questions.explanation: A's last word on it is that a skip filled heaped rather than level will simply be refused when the lorry comes.

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker say households fail?
options: On food rather than on water
On water rather than on food
On batteries and torches
On knowing their neighbours
questions.correctAnswer: On water rather than on food
questions.explanation: Most households already hold three days of food without trying; water is the thing they get wrong.

questions.prompt: How much water does a family of four need for three days?
options: Twelve litres
Four litres
Seventy-two litres
Forty-eight litres
questions.correctAnswer: Forty-eight litres
questions.explanation: Four litres per person per day, covering drinking and washing, comes to forty-eight litres for four people over three days — which is why containers are suggested rather than bottles.

questions.prompt: When should the gas be turned off?
options: As a precaution whenever a warning is issued
Whenever the household leaves the house
Only if gas can be smelt or the building has moved
Only after the utility has been telephoned
questions.correctAnswer: Only if gas can be smelt or the building has moved
questions.explanation: Turning it off as a precaution is specifically warned against, because only the utility can turn it back on and that has taken two weeks after a large event.

questions.prompt: Why does the second meeting point matter more?
options: The likelier problem is not being able to get back into the area
The first is usually too close to the house
Neighbours can be relied on to gather there
It is easier for children to remember
questions.correctAnswer: The likelier problem is not being able to get back into the area
questions.explanation: The failure case the speaker has in mind is not a house fire but being unable to get back into the neighbourhood at all, which is what the second point is for.

questions.prompt: Why should people text rather than telephone?
options: Texts are cheaper during an emergency
Texts queue and go through when calls fail
Calls are reserved for emergency services
Texts can be sent without a signal
questions.correctAnswer: Texts queue and go through when calls fail
questions.explanation: Calls fail on a loaded network while texts queue and eventually go through — the same network behaving differently.

questions.prompt: What is the block list for?
options: Listing which households have supplies
Keeping a record of who is away
Deciding who checks on whom
Recording who might need help getting downstairs
questions.correctAnswer: Recording who might need help getting downstairs
questions.explanation: The speaker is explicit that nobody has to become friends: the list exists to record who might need help getting down stairs.

questions.prompt: What is being capped?
options: Class sizes in the earliest grades
The number of teachers a board may hire
Class sizes in every grade
The number of portables a school may use
questions.correctAnswer: Class sizes in the earliest grades
questions.explanation: The cap is twenty-two students from kindergarten through grade three, funded for about nine hundred additional teachers.

questions.prompt: Why does the cap stop at grade three?
options: Older classes are already below the cap
Secondary teachers were not consulted
The benefit of smaller classes is largest in the earliest grades
The funding runs out above grade three
questions.correctAnswer: The benefit of smaller classes is largest in the earliest grades
questions.explanation: The province says the evidence shows the effect of smaller classes is largest early and fades as students get older.

questions.prompt: What is the first practical problem boards raise?
options: Parents will move children between schools
There are no spare rooms in the fastest-growing suburbs
The cap is set too low to be useful
Boards cannot afford the additional salaries
questions.correctAnswer: There are no spare rooms in the fastest-growing suburbs
questions.explanation: A smaller class needs a room, and the boards growing fastest have none left — meaning portables and a capital cost the announcement does not cover.

questions.prompt: What is the second?
options: Nine hundred teachers is fewer than are needed
Teachers would have to be retrained
The September start date is too early
Nine hundred teachers is more than the province graduates in a year
questions.correctAnswer: Nine hundred teachers is more than the province graduates in a year
questions.explanation: Recruitment is the second problem: the province's faculties do not graduate nine hundred teachers in a year.

questions.prompt: Why will the province sample without notice during the year?
options: Boards have refused to report their numbers
The September date falls before enrolment closes
A single count date invites a class to be balanced for one day
The teachers' association asked for it
questions.correctAnswer: A single count date invites a class to be balanced for one day
questions.explanation: Compliance is measured on the thirtieth of September, and some boards say that invites a class to be balanced for that day and then left alone, so the province will also sample twice unannounced.

questions.prompt: What is the choice before them?
options: Two possible locations for the same crossing
A crossing this year or two next year
A speed table or a lower speed limit
A signalled crossing or a raised speed table
questions.correctAnswer: A signalled crossing or a raised speed table
questions.explanation: Sindhu opens with two options and money for one: a signalled crossing at thirty-eight thousand, or a raised speed table at nine.

questions.prompt: How does Oduya distinguish them?
options: The crossing is quicker to install
The table slows all traffic; the crossing protects one place
The table needs less maintenance
The crossing works only during school hours
questions.correctAnswer: The table slows all traffic; the crossing protects one place
questions.explanation: Oduya's distinction is that the crossing gives a protected place to cross, while the table slows everybody along the stretch — including drivers who would never stop at a crossing.

questions.prompt: What is Ntuli's objection to the plan?
options: Her children cross at the corner, not where the crossing would go
The crossing would be too far from the school gate
Her children are too young to use a crossing
The corner is already the most dangerous point
questions.correctAnswer: Her children cross at the corner, not where the crossing would go
questions.explanation: Ntuli's children cross forty metres up at the corner, because that is where the path comes out — so a crossing on the plan's site would sit unused beside them.

questions.prompt: Why can the crossing not go at the corner itself?
options: The path is on private land
The road is too narrow there
Sight lines
It would block a bus stop
questions.correctAnswer: Sight lines
questions.explanation: Oduya rules out the corner itself on sight lines, while accepting that ten metres back would be better than the location on the plan.

questions.prompt: What does Oduya concede about crossings?
options: They are ineffective outside schools
They need to be signalled to work at all
They cost more to maintain than a table
A third of people will not walk to one that is off their line
questions.correctAnswer: A third of people will not walk to one that is off their line
questions.explanation: Oduya's honest answer is that a crossing works when it is on people's line, and moving it twenty metres off that line loses about a third of them.

questions.prompt: What is the argument for the table?
options: It can be installed at the corner
It is more popular with residents
It works whether or not anybody cooperates
It slows traffic only at school times
questions.correctAnswer: It works whether or not anybody cooperates
questions.explanation: Sindhu puts it and Oduya agrees: the table works without cooperation — while adding that this is also the argument against treating it as sufficient by itself.

questions.prompt: What does Ntuli propose doing with the money left over?
options: Building a footpath from the corner to the crossing point
Adding a second speed table further along
Holding it for the crossing next year
Paying for a crossing guard
questions.correctAnswer: Building a footpath from the corner to the crossing point
questions.explanation: Ntuli would take the table and ask what a footpath from the corner to the crossing point costs — which Oduya prices at under ten thousand, deliverable in the same season.

questions.prompt: What is decided?
options: The crossing now, with the table next year
The table and the path now, with the crossing next year
The table alone, with the saving returned
Nothing, pending a further report
questions.correctAnswer: The table and the path now, with the crossing next year
questions.explanation: Sindhu closes with the table plus the path this year, and the crossing on next year's list with the path already built.

questions.prompt: What reduction do the best studies find?
options: Between two and eight per cent of a meal
About a quarter of a meal
Between twenty and eighty calories a meal
No measurable reduction at all
questions.correctAnswer: Between twenty and eighty calories a meal
questions.explanation: The studies comparing covered chains against uncovered ones find a reduction of somewhere between twenty and eighty calories per meal.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker compare that reduction to?
options: About one bite of a burger
A single soft drink
One meal a month
A quarter of a portion
questions.correctAnswer: About one bite of a burger
questions.explanation: The speaker calls the reduction real and measurable, and then puts it at roughly one bite of a burger — close to nothing against the scale of the problem.

questions.prompt: What changed the speaker's view of the policy?
options: A larger study with better data
Its effect on the menus rather than on customers
The cost of enforcing it
Evidence from countries that repealed it
questions.correctAnswer: Its effect on the menus rather than on customers
questions.explanation: The measurable effect on customers is small, but the effect on the menus is not — which is the part the speaker says changed their view.

questions.prompt: What did the chains do once covered by the rules?
options: Raised prices on their highest-calorie items
Printed the counts in smaller type
Reduced the size of their menus overall
Cut portions, changed recipes, and dropped their highest-calorie items
questions.correctAnswer: Cut portions, changed recipes, and dropped their highest-calorie items
questions.explanation: Chains under the rules reformulated: smaller portions, changed recipes, and several quietly withdrew their highest-calorie items rather than print the number beside them.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker call that mechanism more durable?
options: It applies to small restaurants as well
It cannot be reversed by a later government
It works whether or not customers look at the numbers
It saves the chains money
questions.correctAnswer: It works whether or not customers look at the numbers
questions.explanation: The supply-side mechanism is more durable than the demand-side one precisely because it works whether or not customers read the numbers.

questions.prompt: What cost does the speaker say should be named?
options: The cost to chains of reprinting menus
The loss of popular items customers wanted
The expense of monitoring compliance
The documented harm to people with eating disorders
questions.correctAnswer: The documented harm to people with eating disorders
questions.explanation: The cost worth naming falls on people with eating disorders, for whom an unavoidable number on every item is a documented harm — not a reason to abandon the policy, but a reason to stop calling it free.
